$$
\newcommand{\Exp}{\text{Exp}(\lambda)}
\newcommand{\Geo}{\text{Geometric}(p)}
\newcommand{\expCdf}[1]{F_{\lambda}(#1)}
\newcommand{\geoCdf}[1]{H_{p}(#1)}
$$
I have known for a some time that the [geometric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_distribution) and [exponential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_distribution) distributions are related, with both being the only two memoryless distributions on discrete and continuous time [@pitman-93], respectively, and the former being often presented as the discrete counterpart to the former.

In this little writeup, I try to clarify the exact nature of this relationship. In particular, we will take an exponential distribution $\Exp$ with rate parameter $\lambda$ and attempt to discretize it into a geometric distribution $\Geo$ with parameter $p$.

**Discretizing.** So, what does "discretizing" mean in our context? We start by slicing the positive real numbers into fixed-sized, countably infinitely many intervals $d_i = [(i - 1) \Delta t, i \Delta t)$ of length $\Delta t$ each. Now let $F_{\lambda}(x)$ and $H_{p}(x)$ be the cumulative distribution functions for $\Exp$ and $\Geo$, respectively. Given a rate $\lambda$, we want to show that there exists a single $p$ such that:

$$
F_{\lambda}(d_i) = H_{p}(i)
$$

for all $i \geq 1$. If we can show that, we are effectively demonstrating that the distributions accumulate mass at the same rate, but $H_p$ does so in discrete jumps instead of continuously. 

By construction, we know that:

$$
F_{\lambda}(x) = 1 - e^{-\lambda x} \qquad
F_{p}(i) = 1 - (1 - p)^{i}
$$
Then:

$$
1 - (1-p)^i = 1 - e^{\lambda i\Delta t} \iff p = 1 - e^{-\frac{\lambda i \Delta t}{i}} \overset{*}{\iff} p = 1 - e^{-\lambda\Delta t}
$$ {#eq-p}

The most important part here is the starred step (*) showing that the $i$ cancels out, meaning that $p$ is the same for all $i_\blacksquare$. Let's now plot this out and see how this looks like. We compute the parameter $p$ from $\lambda$ as in Eq. [-@eq-p] using $\lambda = 2$, and $\Delta t = 0.2$:








::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_cdfs(
  cdfs(lambda = 2, delta_t = 0.2, xmax = 4)
)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Cumulative distribution functions for $F_{\lambda}(x)$ and $H_{p}(x)$ with $\lambda = 2$, $\Delta t = 0.2$, $p = 1 - e^{-0.4}$.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cdfs-1.png){#fig-cdfs fig-align='center' width=960}
:::
:::


And we see that, indeed, naming the geometric distribution is a discrete counterpart to the exponential makes sense.
